summary: A revision to the appendix of BBN Report 1822 that lists sites on the ARPANET, now written to include sites about to join. BBN urged hosts to add new sites to their local address tables quickly. It also argued that a host program should not drop valid messages just because the sender is missing from a table.

eli5.summary: Imagine a phone book that also lists people who are about to move in. This note asks everyone to add the new neighbors early, and not to hang up on callers just because they are not yet in the book.

subtitle: Network address directory for ARPANET sites

tldr.problem: Many ARPANET hosts required local address tables before accepting messages from unknown senders. As the network grew and new sites joined regularly, these tables became outdated and restricted communication.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 208 publishes the address assignments for all connected and near-future sites, organized by IMP number, host number, and network address. It urges hosts to update their tables proactively and argues against rejecting valid messages based on missing address entries.
tldr.outcome: This directory became one of the first ARPANET site lists. Later, DNS and centralized registries replaced local address tables.

facts.label: Author
facts.value: A. McKenzie, Bolt Beranek and Newman

today: RFC 208 is a historical snapshot of the ARPANET address space in summer 1971. The network soon outgrew static tables. The transition to DNS (Domain Name System) in the 1980s replaced local address lists with dynamic, hierarchical name resolution. This early RFC documents one of the ARPANET's first operational directories.

sections.title: Address Assignment and Tables
sections.content:
RFC 208 publishes the first comprehensive ARPANET host address directory. A network address in the ARPA Network is encoded in the Host-to-IMP message leader: bits 9-10 specify a host number (0-3) attached to an IMP, and bits 11-16 specify the IMP number (1-31). Together they form an 8-bit network address that identifies each host.

BBN recommended treating this directory as prospective rather than retrospective: it includes sites scheduled for imminent connection, not just those currently online. This allows hosts to add new sites to their local tables immediately, reducing delays when a new site comes online.
sections.eli5: Each computer on the ARPANET gets a number made of two parts: which machine it is plugged into (IMP number) and which port on that machine (host number). The note lists all of them.

sections.title: The Site Directory
sections.content:
RFC 208 tabulates the IMP numbers, host numbers, network addresses, and scheduled installation dates. At publication in August 1971, fifteen sites are connected: UCLA (IMP 1), SRI (2), UCSB (3), Utah (4), BBN (5), MIT (6), RAND (7), SDC (8), Harvard (9), Lincoln (10), Stanford (11), Illinois (12), CASE (13), Carnegie-Mellon (14), and Burroughs/Illiac (15). Additional sites from NASA/Ames through BBN/TIP are scheduled through March 1972.

The RFC also notes a critical address change at BBN: prior to September 1, 1971, the PDP-10 (A) will be Host 0; after that date it becomes Host 1, and the DDP-516 moves from Host 1 to Host 0.
sections.eli5: Fifteen computers are on the net in August 1971. Ten more are about to join. Every few weeks, a new one plugs in.

sections.title: Argument Against Address Filtering
sections.content:
RFC 208 argues that it is irrational for an NCP (Network Control Program) to discard valid messages simply because the sender's address does not appear in the local table. It is equally irrational to prevent a local user from attempting communication with a remote site whose address is known to the user but missing from the NCP's tables.

This critique foreshadows the later shift toward more open network routing and dynamic discovery, rather than requiring prior knowledge of all possible peers.
sections.eli5: The note argues: do not reject mail from addresses not in your table. Let people talk even if the other person is new.
